desc:
A grid describes a gold mine: grid[r][c] is the amount of gold in that cell, and 0 means the cell is empty rock.

You choose any cell that holds gold as the start, and then walk. Each step goes to a neighbouring cell (up, down, left or right) that holds gold. You collect the gold of every cell you step on, but you may not step on the same cell twice, and you may stop at any moment. Return the largest total amount of gold you can collect, or 0 if the mine has no gold.

grid = [[0,3,0],
        [4,9,5],
        [0,2,0]]   -> 18
grid = [[2,2],
        [2,2]]     -> 8

In the first example the best walk is 4, 9, 5. In the second example the walk can go around all four cells.
hints: The walk may turn in any direction, so a greedy choice of the largest neighbour does not work.
Try every starting cell and explore every possible walk from it. With at most 18 gold cells the number of walks is small enough.
Use backtracking: take the gold of the current cell (set it to 0 to mark it as used), recurse into the four neighbours that still hold gold, then restore the cell before returning.
editorial: This is a depth-first search with backtracking. From each gold cell, collect its gold and temporarily set the cell to zero, so that it cannot be entered again on the current walk. Then try each of the four neighbours that still have gold and keep the best total returned by them. Finally restore the original value so that other walks can use the cell.

The answer is the best value over all starting cells. In the worst case a walk visits all 18 gold cells, but because gold cells are capped, the number of simple walks in a grid is small enough to enumerate (a full 4 × 4 block has only a few thousand simple walks). The time is exponential in the number of gold cells, O(k · 3<sup>k</sup>), and the space is O(k) for the recursion.
